item.title: By: Matthew Logan
item.dc:creator: Matthew Logan
item.description:
Hi Carl. I may pick up a copy of Lau's translation. In comparing the two chapters from your recent weeks reading, they do seem quite different. A book I picked up this year called 'The Unencumbered Spirit' by Hung Yung-ming (tran. by W.Scott Wilson) is proving quite interesting to use for the occasional look-through. It's less, I guess one might say, scripture than the Tao Te Ching and more poetic in form.
I think one of the great things about mountain music is that the original message or theme of the songs remains, even though sometimes it is viewed through a Christian or gospel lens. As you say, they point to the universal human condition.
The notion of a wayfaring stranger wandering through a lonesome valley seems appropriate to both Taoism and Christianity, though maybe the Christian has a clearer idea of his destination where the Taoist is more content to wander until his destination presents itself.
Regards,
Matt

item.title: By: carl
item.dc:creator: carl
item.description:
Yes, Wayfaring stranger is another one. Lots of the gospel songs convey the human condition well if you 'translate' the Christian views they express. By 'translate' I mean, see the views as symptoms of the universal human condition.
On translations: the D.C. Lau one is quite faithful the actual Chinese. He does take liberties so as to make it more poetic English-wise. Mitchell's, on the other hand, is not a translation from the actual Chinese but an interpretation of various translations. This is true of many so called translations, and may be why they tend to be more humanistic and politically correct compared to the contrariety of the original.

item.title: By: Matthew Logan
item.dc:creator: Matthew Logan
item.description:
Thanks Carl.
I really like the version of the Tao Te Ching which you use, it has quite a different flavour to my copy (tran. by Stephen Mitchell), though the spirit behind the words is the same.
"The Master...lets himself be shaped by the Tao/ as rugged and common as a stone."
'Lonesome Valley'. I'll check that one out. It will certainly make a change from me banging out 'Cripple Creek' all the time at jams! 'Wayfaring Stranger' seems to be a song in a similar vein too.
Best Regards,
Matt

item.title: By: Matthew Logan
item.dc:creator: Matthew Logan
item.description:
Hi Carl, Thanks for making this available for folks to read and use. I took up hatha yoga earlier this year after being inspired by watching you and Kyle practice together.
I suffer from asthma which tends to get worse in Winter and puts me off running and other aerobic stuff which I do try to do in Summer, so I was looking for a replacement exercise. I also dislike gyms and much prefer to practice on my own, and in my own space.
I started out with a copy of 'Light On Yoga' but I've now replaced that with your manual. It is a bit more accessible for me as a beginner, and I'm finding the hints and tips from an experienced practitioner useful.
I'm happily working on the first program, and I'm finding the postures there a great challenge. I found that sitting in Zazen was difficult, but hatha yoga really does seem to exemplify the idea of 'moving meditation'!
I seem to be learning much from your family's teachings and examples. It does feel kinda lonely in the UK sometimes as far as taoist folks and those mindful of the way go, so I'll endeavour to post here more often.
Thanks again.
Best Regards,
Matthew, UK
